lessons.title: Identifying who buys blocks: builders, NGOs, and homeowners
lessons.body:
Before you make a single block for sale, you must know who will buy it. In most African towns, there are three main groups: builders (contractors and fundis), NGOs, and homeowners. Each buys differently.

Builders are your biggest customers. They buy in bulkâ500, 1000, or 5000 blocks at a time. They care about price per block, consistent quality, and delivery speed. A builder working on a school or church project needs blocks on site every morning. If you can supply 500 blocks daily at a fair price, you become their go-to. Builders often pay cash or a 50% deposit. They will inspect your blocks for cracks and correct curing.

NGOs and government projects buy through tenders or quotations. They need receipts, sometimes a registered business, and they pay by cheque or bank transfer after delivery. A single NGO order can be 2000 blocks for a health centre. To win them, you must provide a written quotation with your price per block, delivery cost, and timeline. NGOs value reliability and often ask for samples first. They may also require blocks that meet specific strength standards.

Homeowners buy smaller numbersâ50 to 300 blocksâfor a house, a boundary wall, or a pit latrine. They pay cash and often carry blocks themselves or hire a pickup. Homeowners care about appearance (smooth edges, uniform colour) and personal service. They will tell neighbours about you if you treat them well. A homeowner who buys 100 blocks today may buy 500 next year.

To find these buyers, visit building sites, talk to fundis at hardware stores, and leave your number with local chiefs and church leaders. Keep a notebook with names, phone numbers, and what they bought. Your first 10 customers will come from people you already know. Ask each one: âWho else do you know who needs blocks?â That question alone can double your sales.

lessons.title: Creating simple flyers and WhatsApp messages to advertise
lessons.body:
You do not need a computer or a professional designer to make a flyer. A flyer is just a piece of paper that tells people what you sell, where you are, and how to reach you. Use a pen and a ruler to make a neat template, then photocopy it at a local shop for 100 shillings per page. Print 100 copiesâthat is enough to start.

Your flyer must have five things: (1) Your business name, e.g., âKato Blocks & Cement.â (2) What you sell: â6-inch and 4-inch blocks, cured for 14 days.â (3) Your price: â6-inch block = 2,500 UGX.â (4) Your location: âNear Kalerwe Market, after the mosque.â (5) Your phone number and WhatsApp. Add a simple drawing of a block with a checkmark. Keep it black and white to save money.

WhatsApp is your most powerful free tool. Create a broadcast list of every builder, fundi, and homeowner you meet. Send one message per week, not more. A good message is short: âHello, this is Kato Blocks. We have 2000 fresh 6-inch blocks ready. Price 2,500 each. Free delivery within 5 km. Call 0777-123456.â Add a photo of your blocks stacked neatly. Photos sell better than words.

Use WhatsApp Status to show your work. Post a 10-second video of your block-making machine in action, or a customer loading blocks onto a truck. Post at 7 AM and 6 PM when people check their phones. Add a caption: âOrder today, get blocks tomorrow.â

Do not spam people. If someone says âstop,â remove them. Instead, ask happy customers to forward your message to their friends. Offer a small reward: âIf you bring a friend who buys 100 blocks, you get 10 blocks free.â This turns your customers into your advertising team. A single flyer or WhatsApp message can bring you 5 new orders in a week if it is clear and honest.

lessons.title: Showing samples and inviting customers to your yard
lessons.body:
People buy what they can see and touch. Your yard is your showroom. Even if it is small, make it look professional. Clear the grass, stack blocks neatly by size, and keep a few âdisplay blocksâ on a wooden table. Display blocks should be clean, smooth, and free of cracks. Paint one block half-red and half-white to show your colour options if you offer coloured blocks.

When a customer arrives, greet them and offer a seat. Give them a sample block to hold. Say: âFeel the weight. Tap itâit rings like a bell. That means it is well-cured and strong.â Show them how a block fits together with another block. If you have a hammer, break a reject block to show the inside is solid, not hollow. This builds trust.

Invite customers to your yard through WhatsApp and flyers. Write: âVisit our yard at [location] any day between 8 AM and 5 PM. See our blocks, touch them, and get a free sample piece.â For builders, offer to deliver a free sample of 5 blocks to their site. For homeowners, offer a 10% discount if they come to the yard themselves.

Keep a visitor book. Write down every personâs name, phone number, and what they asked about. Follow up within two days: âHello, this is Kato. You visited my yard on Tuesday. Did you like the blocks? I can deliver 200 blocks tomorrow.â This follow-up turns a visitor into a buyer.

Make your yard easy to find. Put a signboard at the nearest main road with an arrow: âBlocks â 200m.â If you are near a market, tell the market chairman to announce your yard. A clean, well-organised yard with samples ready will sell more blocks than any radio advert. Customers trust what they see with their own eyes.

lessons.title: Building relationships with local hardware stores and contractors
lessons.body:
Hardware stores and contractors are your best salespeople. They already have customers who need blocks. Your job is to make it easy for them to sell your blocks and make a profit.

Start with hardware stores. Visit every hardware store within 5 km of your yard. Ask to speak to the owner. Say: âI make quality blocks. I will give you a 10% commission on every block you sell for me. You do not pay me until the customer pays you.â Leave 5 sample blocks with a price list. The store owner will display your blocks next to their cement and iron sheets. When a customer buys cement, the owner says, âYou also need blocks? I have Katoâs blocksâ2,500 each.â You only pay commission after the sale. This costs you nothing upfront.

Contractors are different. They buy directly from you, but they need credit and reliability. Offer a contractor a special price: âIf you buy 1000 blocks, I will give you 2,300 per block and free delivery.â Ask for a 50% deposit. Deliver on time, every time. If you promise blocks at 8 AM, be there at 7:30 AM. One late delivery can lose a contractor forever. Build a relationship by visiting their site, asking about their project, and solving problems. If they need 200 blocks urgently, find a way to supply them even if you have to borrow from another maker.

Keep a list of all hardware stores and contractors. Call them every two weeks. Ask: âDo you have any customers who need blocks this week?â Send them a WhatsApp message with a photo of your latest stack. Remember their birthdays or important days. Small giftsâa soda, a packet of biscuitsâbuild loyalty.

Never bypass a hardware store to sell directly to their customer. That destroys trust. Instead, thank the store owner and give them their commission quickly. A good relationship with three hardware stores and two contractors can keep you busy full-time. Treat them as partners, not just buyers.

lessons.title: Using word-of-mouth and testimonials to get more orders
lessons.body:
Word-of-mouth is the cheapest and most powerful marketing. In Africa, people trust their neighbours more than adverts. One happy customer can bring you ten new ones. Your job is to make every customer happy and then ask them to tell others.

After you deliver blocks, wait two days and call the customer. Ask: âDid the blocks work well? Are you satisfied?â If they say yes, ask for a testimonial. Say: âCan I write down what you said and use it to show other customers?â Write their exact words: âKatoâs blocks are strong. My wall has no cracks.â Add their name and village. Keep a notebook of testimonials. When a new customer visits your yard, show them the notebook. Say: âLook, Mr. Ochieng from Bweyogerere bought 500 blocks. This is what he said.â That is more convincing than any flyer.

Ask for referrals directly. After a happy customer pays, say: âIf you know one person who needs blocks, give them my number. If they buy 100 blocks, I will give you 10 blocks free.â This reward system works. Most people will tell at least one friend. Give the reward only after the new customer pays. Keep a record of who referred whom.

Use WhatsApp groups. Join local community groups, church groups, and savings groups. Do not spam. Instead, post a photo of a finished wall built with your blocks and write: âThis wall was built with my blocks. The owner is happy. Call me for your blocks.â When someone comments, reply politely and ask them to visit your yard.

Create a simple âcustomer of the monthâ photo. Take a picture of a happy customer standing next to their new wall. Post it on your WhatsApp Status and on a notice board at the market. Ask the customer for permission first. A real face and a real wall sell more than a thousand words. Word-of-mouth grows slowly at first, then suddenly. Keep every customer happy, and your order book will fill itself.

lessons.title: Handling customer complaints and returns professionally
lessons.body:
Complaints are not attacksâthey are chances to keep a customer for life. How you handle a complaint matters more than the original mistake. Always stay calm, listen, and never argue.

When a customer complains, first say: âThank you for telling me. I am sorry you are not happy. Let me fix it.â Do not blame the customer or the weather. Ask questions: âWhich blocks are broken? How many? Can I see them?â If the customer brings back broken blocks, count them. If it is your faultâfor example, you sold under-cured blocksâreplace them free of charge. Give new blocks immediately, even if you have to take them from another order. A customer who gets a free replacement will tell everyone you are honest.

Set a clear return policy and write it on your receipt. For example: âWe replace any block that breaks within 7 days of delivery if it was not damaged by the customer. Bring the broken block to our yard.â This protects you from people who break blocks themselves and want free ones. If a customer claims a block broke during normal use, ask to see the wall. If the block was laid properly and still broke, replace it. If the customer dropped it or used it as a hammer, politely explain that is not covered.

For large orders, offer a discount on the next order instead of a cash refund. Say: âI cannot refund cash, but I will give you 50 free blocks on your next order of 500.â This keeps the money in your business and keeps the customer coming back. Always follow up after solving a complaint: âHello, did the new blocks work well? Are you happy now?â If they say yes, ask them to tell others.

Keep a complaint book. Write down the date, customer name, problem, and how you solved it. Look for patterns. If three customers complain about the same size block, fix your mould. Complaints are free lessons. Handle them professionally, and your reputation will grow stronger than any advert.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Marketing and Selling Your Blocks

In African cement and block enterprises, production capacity is rarely the main constraint on growth. Demand generation is. A block yard with 2,000 units in stock and no order book is a cash-flow crisis waiting to happen, while a yard that sells out weekly can reinvest in moulds, curing space, and transport. This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a working system you can apply from the first day of operation. It assumes you are producing solid or hollow cement blocks, whether manually with a vibrating table or semi-automatically, and selling into a local or regional market.

Marketing blocks is not the same as marketing a branded consumer product. Your buyers are practical, price-sensitive, and risk-averse. They care about block strength, dimensional consistency, delivery reliability, and whether you will still be in business when they need a replacement. The system below is built around those realities: identify the buyer, communicate clearly, prove quality with samples, build a repeat network, and handle problems without losing the relationship.

1. Who Buys Your Blocks â and What They Actually Want

Your market is not "everyone who needs blocks." It is three distinct segments, each with different buying triggers, payment behaviour, and quality expectations. Builders and contractors buy in volume, negotiate hard, and care about delivery timing and consistent strength. NGOs, churches, and community projects buy against a budget line, require quotations and sometimes receipts for accountability, and often pay on delivery or after milestone approval. Homeowners buy in smaller quantities, are more sensitive to unit price and appearance, and often decide based on a neighbour's recommendation or a WhatsApp photo.

Table 1: Buyer segments, buying triggers, and sales approach
Segment Typical order size Main buying trigger Sales approach that works
Builders & contractors 500â10,000+ blocks Project start date, site access, price per unit Direct visit to site, volume discount, guaranteed delivery date
NGOs, churches, schools 1,000â20,000 blocks Approved budget, donor reporting deadline Formal written quotation, receipts, ability to invoice
Homeowners 50â800 blocks Starting a room, wall, or extension WhatsApp photos, yard visit, small-quantity delivery
Hardware stores 200â2,000 blocks (resale) Customer demand, shelf space, margin Trade price, consignment or credit terms, regular restock

Sources: ILO Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) training materials; Global Alliance for Building and Construction, Africa Construction Market Review; field guidance from Enterprise Uganda and Kenya's Micro and Small Enterprises Authority (MSEA).

2. Simple Flyers and WhatsApp Messages That Get Replies

You do not need a graphic designer. A flyer that works in an African block market has five elements: business name and location, block types and sizes, price per unit (or "from" price), a phone number that is answered, and one proof point such as "over 50,000 blocks delivered since 2021." Print A5 size, double-sided if you can afford it, and distribute at hardware stores, building sites, churches, and market days.

WhatsApp is your highest-return channel because it is free, visual, and already used by nearly every buyer. A working format is: one clear photo of stacked blocks, a short caption with price and location, and a call to action. For example: "Solid 6-inch blocks, KES 55 each. Yard at Kiambu Road. Free delivery over 500 blocks. Call 07XX XXX XXX." Post the same message to your status every two to three days, and save every customer's number under a tag like "Block Buyer â Kiambu."

â  SAFETY AND COMPLIANCE WARNING

Never advertise a block strength or load-bearing capacity you have not actually tested. In many African markets, building codes and local authorities require blocks to meet a minimum compressive strength (often 3.5â7 N/mmÂ² for hollow blocks and higher for load-bearing walls). Selling under-strength blocks for structural walls has caused wall collapses, injuries, and deaths, and exposes you to criminal liability and business closure. If you claim "high strength," keep test records from a recognised laboratory or a documented cube-crush test. Also confirm your local council's registration, environmental, and workplace safety requirements before scaling up.

3. Samples, Yard Visits, and the Power of Touch

Blocks are a tactile product. Buyers want to lift one, check the corners, and see whether it rings when tapped. Invite every serious enquirer to your yard. Keep a "sample stack" of your best blocks near the entrance, with a small sign showing the size, price, and curing date. Offer a free single block to contractors and hardware stores as a trial â the cost is trivial compared with the value of a repeat order.

During a yard visit, walk the customer through your curing process. Explaining that blocks are water-cured for at least 7â14 days builds confidence and justifies your price against cheaper, uncured competitors. Give them a written quotation on the spot, and follow up on WhatsApp within 24 hours.

4. Building Relationships with Hardware Stores and Contractors

Hardware stores are a distribution channel, not just a customer. A store that stocks your blocks gives you shelf space, credibility, and a steady trickle of homeowner buyers. Offer a trade price that leaves the retailer a 15â25% margin, agree a restock rhythm, and provide a small branded sign or price tag for their display. Visit at least monthly, check stock levels, and replace damaged units.

Contractors are your highest-value repeat buyers. Keep a simple contact list with their project pipeline, preferred block size, and payment terms. A contractor who trusts you will call you first for the next site. Small gestures â a quick delivery, a replacement for a broken block, a flexible payment window on a large order â build loyalty far more effectively than discounts alone.

5. Word-of-Mouth and Testimonials

In most African towns, reputation travels faster than advertising. After every completed order, ask the customer for a short testimonial â a sentence and a photo is enough. Post it on WhatsApp status and on a simple Facebook page. Keep a notebook or phone note of every referral source so you know which relationships are generating business.

Table 2: Low-cost marketing channels ranked by cost and reach for a small block yard
Channel Relative cost Typical reach Best for
WhatsApp status & groups Very low High (local) Homeowners, referrals, repeat buyers
Printed flyers (A5) Low Medium Site workers, market days, hardware stores
Yard signage & sample stack Low (one-off) Medium Walk-in traffic, passing contractors
Hardware store partnership Medium (margin) High (steady) Homeowners, small builders
Community radio spot Medium High (regional) NGOs, churches, large projects
Facebook / Marketplace Low Mediumâhigh Homeowners, diaspora-funded builds

Sources: GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa reports on WhatsApp usage; ILO SIYB marketing module; UN-Habitat guidance on local building-materials supply chains.

6. Handling Complaints and Returns Professionally

Complaints are inevitable. The way you handle them determines whether you keep the customer and protect your reputation. Follow a simple four-step response: listen without interrupting, acknowledge the problem, agree a specific remedy and timeline, and follow up to confirm the customer is satisfied. Common complaints in block sales include broken units on delivery, wrong size, late delivery, and inconsistent strength. For broken units, replace them on the next delivery or refund the value â do not argue over a few blocks. For quality disputes, invite the customer to the yard, inspect the batch together, and if the fault is yours, replace or refund without delay.

Keep a written record of every complaint, the cause, and the resolution. Patterns will reveal production or delivery problems you can fix â for example, poor stacking during transport causing breakages, or insufficient curing causing weak blocks. A customer whose complaint is resolved well often becomes your most loyal advocate.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Identify your three main buyer segments and keep a contact list for each.
  • Print A5 flyers with name, location, block sizes, price, and a phone number that is always answered.
  • Post a clear block photo and price on WhatsApp status at least three times a week.
  • Keep a clean sample stack at the yard entrance and invite every serious enquirer to visit.
  • Sign up at least two hardware stores as resellers and restock them monthly.
  • Collect one testimonial or photo after every completed order.
  • Respond to every complaint within 24 hours and record the cause and resolution.
  • Never claim a strength or certification you cannot prove with a test record.

Further Reading

  • ILO â Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) programme (free training materials on marketing and business management for small enterprises).
  • GSMA Mobile for Development â Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa (free reports on mobile and WhatsApp usage in African markets).
  • UN-Habitat â Building materials and local supply chains (free publications on affordable housing and construction materials in Africa).
  • Micro and Small Enterprises Authority (MSEA), Kenya (free guides and business development services for small enterprises).
  • Enterprise Uganda (free business development and marketing resources for small enterprises in East Africa).

quiz.q: Which group of buyers typically buys blocks in the largest bulk quantities?
quiz.explanation: Builders and contractors buy in bulk (500 to 5000 blocks) for construction projects.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of selling blocks to NGOs?
options: C) They pay by cheque or bank transfer after delivery
D) They buy only 10 blocks at a time
quiz.explanation: NGOs often pay through formal channels like cheques or bank transfers after delivery.

quiz.q: Why do homeowners often care more about appearance than builders?
options: A) They use blocks for decoration only
B) They build small structures where visible quality matters
C) They do not care about strength
D) They always buy coloured blocks
quiz.explanation: Homeowners build houses and walls where smooth, uniform blocks are visible to everyone.

quiz.q: What is the best way to find your first block buyers?
options: A) Wait for them to come to your yard
C) Visit building sites and talk to local fundis
quiz.explanation: Visiting sites and talking to fundis directly connects you with active builders.

quiz.q: What question can double your sales by leveraging your existing customers?
options: A) âCan I have a discount?â
B) âWho else do you know who needs blocks?â
C) âWhy did you buy from me?â
D) âDo you want a refund?â
quiz.explanation: Asking for referrals turns one happy customer into multiple new leads.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five essential things on a block-selling flyer?
quiz.explanation: A flyer needs business name, product, price, location, and contactânot personal preferences.

quiz.q: How often should you send WhatsApp broadcast messages to your customer list?
quiz.explanation: Once a week is enough to stay visible without annoying customers.

quiz.q: What is a good time to post on WhatsApp Status to reach most people?
quiz.explanation: People check their phones in the morning and evening, so those times get more views.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone says âstopâ to your WhatsApp messages?
options: B) Remove them from your list
quiz.explanation: Respecting their request keeps your business professional and avoids being blocked.

quiz.q: What is a simple reward for a customer who brings a friend who buys 100 blocks?
quiz.explanation: Giving 10 free blocks is a low-cost, high-value incentive for referrals.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a few âdisplay blocksâ on a table in your yard?
options: B) To show customers the quality they will get
D) To sell at a higher price
quiz.explanation: Display blocks let customers see and touch the product, building trust.

quiz.q: What does tapping a block and hearing a ringing sound indicate?
options: B) The block is well-cured and strong
quiz.explanation: A clear ring means the block is dense and properly cured.

quiz.q: What is a good way to invite customers to your yard?
options: A) âVisit my yard to see blocks and get a free sample piece.â
B) âStay away from my yard.â
D) âCall before you come, maybe.â
quiz.explanation: Offering a free sample and a clear invitation encourages visits.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a visitor book in your yard?
options: A) To record names and follow up later
B) To show off your handwriting
C) To report people to police
D) To use as a receipt book
quiz.explanation: A visitor book helps you follow up with potential customers within two days.

quiz.q: What is a simple sign to help customers find your yard?
options: A) A billboard on the highway
B) âBlocks â 200mâ at the nearest main road
quiz.explanation: A directional sign near a main road guides customers to your location.

quiz.q: What commission should you offer a hardware store for selling your blocks?
quiz.explanation: A 10% commission is fair and motivates the store to sell your blocks.

quiz.q: When should a hardware store pay you for blocks they sell on your behalf?
options: B) After the customer pays them
quiz.explanation: You only get paid after the sale, so there is no upfront cost to the store.

quiz.q: What special price can you offer a contractor who buys 1000 blocks?
options: B) A discount, e.g., 2,300 per block
C) Same price as single blocks
quiz.explanation: Bulk discounts encourage contractors to buy large quantities.

quiz.q: Why is it important to deliver blocks on time to a contractor?
options: A) Late delivery can lose you the contractor forever
B) Contractors do not care about time
D) They pay extra for late delivery
quiz.explanation: Contractors depend on timely deliveries to keep their projects on schedule.

quiz.q: What should you never do with a hardware storeâs customer?
options: B) Bypass the store and sell directly to the customer
C) Give the store a commission
quiz.explanation: Bypassing the store destroys trust and ruins the relationship.

quiz.q: What is the best way to get a testimonial from a happy customer?
options: A) Write it yourself and pretend it is theirs
B) Ask them to say a few words and write it down
C) Steal their words from a conversation
quiz.explanation: Asking directly and recording their exact words makes the testimonial authentic.

quiz.q: How can you use a testimonial to convince a new customer?
options: A) Show them a notebook with real customer comments
B) Hide it in your pocket
C) Only tell them the price
quiz.explanation: Showing real testimonials builds credibility and trust.

quiz.q: What is a good referral reward for a customer who brings a new buyer?
options: A) A free block for every 10 blocks the new customer buys
quiz.explanation: A proportional reward like 10 free blocks per 100 bought is fair and motivating.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spamming WhatsApp community groups?
options: A) It annoys people and gets you removed
quiz.explanation: Spamming leads to being blocked or removed, losing potential customers.

quiz.q: What is a âcustomer of the monthâ photo used for?
options: A) To show a real happy customer with their wall
C) To advertise a different business
D) To keep for your private album
quiz.explanation: A real photo of a satisfied customer serves as powerful social proof.

quiz.q: When a customer complains, what is the first thing you should say?
options: B) âThank you for telling me. I am sorry. Let me fix it.â
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging the complaint and offering to fix it keeps the customer calm and loyal.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sold under-cured blocks that broke?
options: B) Replace them free of charge
quiz.explanation: Replacing faulty blocks free of charge protects your reputation and builds trust.

quiz.q: What is a fair return policy for blocks?
options: B) Replace any block that breaks within 7 days if not damaged by customer
D) Replace only if customer pays double
quiz.explanation: A clear, limited-time replacement policy is fair and protects both parties.

quiz.q: What is a good alternative to a cash refund for a large order complaint?
options: A) A discount on the next order
B) Telling them to go away
C) Giving them a free T-shirt
quiz.explanation: Offering free blocks or a discount on the next order keeps the money in your business.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a complaint book?
options: A) To identify patterns and fix recurring problems
B) To show off to customers
D) To use as a diary
quiz.explanation: Recording complaints helps you spot trends and improve your product.
